text.p: These are the highlights of the main Sao Paulo and Rio de Janeiro newspapers this morning.
GAZETA MERCANTIL
-- GM ASKS U.S. TO END ACTION AGAINST BRAZIL AUTO RULES
General Motors asked the Clinton administration to end the investigation it launched in October of Brazil's car import rules.
-- BANESPA PREFERRED SHARES ROSE 71 PCT THIS WEEK
Shares of Sao Paulo state bank Banespa surged this week on expectations a solution to the problem of outstanding state debts to the bank has been found, with preferred shares up 71 percent.
-- BRAZIL'S CURRENT ACCOUNT DEFICIT RISES
Brazil's current account deficit rose to 2.89 percent of Gross Domestic Product in October, compared with 2.53 percent in September.
O GLOBO
-- U.S. DENIES VISA TO AIDES OF BRAZIL JUSTICE MINISTER
The United States has denied visas to three Brazilian Justice Ministry officials who had hoped to travel to the U.S. for a seminar on public administration.
-- RAINSTORM IN RIO CAUSES ONE DEATH
A 12-year-old girl was killed and seven others injured when two days of torrential rains in Rio de Janeiro state caused a mudslide in Volta Redonda.
-- OLYMPIC COMMITTEE TEAM ARRIVES IN RIO AMID RAINFALL

A 19-member International Olympic Committee mission evaluating Rio de Janeiro's bid to become the site of the 2004 Olympic Games arrived Thursday amid heavy rainfall and is slated to begin their work today.
FOLHA DE SAO PAULO
-- EXTERNAL DEFICIT REACHES CLOSE TO GOVERNMENT-SET LIMIT

Brazil's current account deficit, the most important indicator of the country's external accounts, has risen to close to the limits sets by the government, rising to $17.233 billion or 2.89 percent of Gross Domestic Product.
-- START OF VALE PRIVATIZATION MAY BE DELAYED TO MARCH

The privatization of Brazilian state mining giant Companhia Vale do Rio Doce, which was to begin in February, may be delayed until March at the request of interested investors, according to the National Development Bank (BNDES).
-- WAR AGAINST EPIDEMICS MAY BE HALTED IN 1997
The war against epidemic diseases, like malaria and dengue, may be interrupted in 1997 due to a lack of funding, the National Health Foundation warned.
Reuters has not verified the stories and cannot vouch for their accuracy.
-- James Craig, Sao Paulo newsroom 5511 232 4411
